title: Houthi Missile Kills 12 at Riyadh Airport as Aramco Moves to Restore Europe Crude
subhead: The deadliest Gulf attack of the Iran war hit Saudi Arabia's main airport and oil infrastructure this week, forcing Riyadh to weigh retaliation while Aramco signals it will restore full crude flows to Europe in November.

sections.heading: Riyadh Airport Struck Again: 12 Dead, 309 Wounded
sections.body:
Saudi civil aviation authorities (GACA) said an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and wounded 309, with some in critical condition, per CNBC and South Korea's SBS. The dead included four Saudi citizens plus nationals of Bangladesh, the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. It is the deadliest strike in any Gulf Arab state since the Iran war began in February.

It was at least the third attack on King Khalid in a week. A missile hit the complex housing domestic Terminals 3 and 4; airport operations were suspended and flights diverted or cancelled, per Flightradar24. Kuwait Airways, Etihad and Qatar Airways all halted Riyadh routes. A projectile also landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, and the Saudi-led coalition said a Houthi ballistic missile was intercepted over Al-Kharj.

A senior Houthi official, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, told the New York Times the group was responsible, calling it retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemeni civilian infrastructure. The Houthis began a declared campaign against Saudi airports and oil facilities on 5 October.
sections.whyItMatters: The attack exposed gaps in Saudi air defenses and hit an economic hub, not a battlefield. That raises the odds Riyadh presses Washington for direct military support at a moment when the US is already militarily committed against Iran.

sections.heading: Trump Weighs Joining Saudi Strikes as Energy Conference Goes Ahead
sections.body:
President Donald Trump said the US is evaluating whether to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis: 'We may. We're going to look at it,' he said Saturday, per CNBC. Al Jazeera reported Trump planned to call Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman after the attack.

Crucially for markets, the Saudi energy ministry pressed ahead with a major international energy conference due to begin in Riyadh, and organisers of two flagship Saudi energy and investment conferences told Reuters the events would proceed with reassurance on security. Riyadh is deliberately signaling that its energy sector and investor calendar remain open for business despite the strikes.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia is trying to decouple a security crisis from an economic-confidence crisis. Whether the conference proceeds without disruption will be read as a test of whether the kingdom can still guarantee the safety of the global energy executives it depends on.

sections.heading: Aramco Signals Full Crude Flows to Europe Are Back in November
sections.body:
Against that backdrop, Saudi Aramco said it will restore full crude oil supplies to Europe in November, according to reporting summarized by Lapaas Voice. The move comes after the recent attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline — the kingdom's key Red Sea export route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz — which Al Jazeera flagged as a compounding factor in the global fuel crunch.

There was no immediate confirmation of the restoration's volume from Aramco's own disclosures in the sources reviewed, so the figure should be read as Aramco's stated intent rather than a verified flow number. Context matters: this is the same week Saudi Arabia unexpectedly cut November oil prices to Asia to six-year lows, per Reuters — a signal Riyadh is still fighting for market share even as its infrastructure is under fire.
sections.whyItMatters: Restoring Europe-bound crude while cutting Asian prices points to a Saudi strategy of defending volumes and customer relationships at almost any cost. Riyadh cannot afford for the war to be read as a supply risk to its own buyers.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Russian Oil Hours After the Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
sections.body:
The Trump administration's diesel arrangement with Moscow is already colliding with the war. Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets immediately, with 500,000 tonnes in November and further tranches after that, per Al Jazeera.

Within hours, Ukraine struck a major Russian oil hub. Kyiv Independent reported a large fire at the Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don, which handles exports from the Novoshakhtinsk refinery (annual capacity 3.5 million tonnes), after a suspected drone attack on 9–10 October. Ukraine separately said it hit Russia's largest oil refinery, per Reuters. Russia partially lifted its diesel export ban after the Trump-Putin deal, Yahoo reported.

Trump responded by calling for Ukraine to replace Zelensky, telling reporters Kyiv 'could have made many deals.' The FT reported the US warned Kyiv that strikes on Russian oil jeopardise intelligence-sharing.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now asking Ukraine to spare the very Russian refining capacity it needs to cool US pump prices — a contradiction Kyiv is visibly unwilling to accept. The diesel deal rests on infrastructure Ukraine is actively destroying.

sections.heading: Why the Diesel Deal May Not Move Prices
sections.body:
Analysts told Al Jazeera the Russian diesel deal will likely have little effect on the global energy crisis, and European countries could refuse to buy Russian product altogether. Trump claimed the combination of the diesel deal and US 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz would lower prices, but a Capital Economics commodities economist, Hamad Hussain, said the earlier G7 release of 100 million barrels of emergency reserves would be 'short-lived.'

US diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon in September — more than double a year earlier — and sits at $6.20 now, per AAA. A House Republican is invoking Ronald Reagan to try to block the 300,000-tonne Russian diesel deal, and Mike Pence publicly urged Trump to rescind it, per MSN aggregations.
sections.whyItMatters: The core problem is refining and logistics, not crude supply. Even a large Russian diesel tranche does little when Hormuz traffic is a fraction of normal and Russian/Ukraine refining capacity is under drone attack — and the politics of buying from Putin are toxic ahead of US midterms.

sections.heading: India Fires a Currency Defenses Shot to Protect Oil Imports
sections.body:
India's central bank unveiled emergency measures to defend the rupee, redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and opening a special dollar window for Indian Oil, HPCL and BPCL, Reuters and Business Standard reported. The rupee has been hovering near record lows as the Iran war inflates the import bill.

India is one of the world's largest crude importers and highly exposed to both price spikes and dollar funding stress. Chinese independent refiners, meanwhile, have been boosting Iraqi oil purchases as Iranian flows fall, per Reuters — showing how Asian buyers are re-wiring supply chains around the Gulf disruption.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the financial channel of the energy crisis: when oil prices and the dollar surge together, import-dependent emerging economies burn reserves to keep fuel flowing. India's move shows the shock is now hitting currency stability, not just trade balances.

sections.heading: Philippines Builds a Strategic Reserve; India Eyes Critical Minerals Stockpile
sections.body:
Two non-Western resilience stories stand out. On 9 October, the Philippine Department of Energy released 'twin roadmaps' — a weekly National Fuel Risk Index and a phased Strategic Petroleum Reserve targeting 60 days of supply initially and 90 days eventually — per an analysis published by Discovery Alert citing regional reporting. It follows the Philippines' State of National Energy Emergency (Executive Order No. 110, in force through March 2027).

Separately, India's Mines Secretary said a national critical minerals stockpiling policy will be finalised within about a month, per Moneycontrol, Business Standard and the Financial Express. It is a direct hedge against the supply-chain fragility exposed by China's export controls on rare earths and battery materials.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz closure is pushing Asian governments to build physical buffers — fuel and mineral reserves — that did not exist before 2026. These are multi-year commitments that treat supply disruption as permanent, not temporary.

bottomLine: The week's defining development is that the Iran war has fully spilled into Saudi Arabia's home front: a missile killed 12 at Riyadh's main airport and struck oil infrastructure, even as Aramco says Europe-bound crude flows will be whole again in November. Riyadh is trying to keep its energy business running while its defenses visibly strain. At the same time, Washington's bid to buy Russian diesel to tame record US prices is being undercut by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries — the product the deal depends on — with Trump now calling for Zelensky's replacement. The common thread across India's dollar defense, the Philippines' reserve roadmaps and China's shift to Iraqi crude is that Asian importers are no longer treating the disruption as a passing shock; they are stockpiling, rationing and re-routing for the long haul.
sources: Reuters, Al Jazeera, CNBC, SBS News (Korea), Kyiv Independent, AP, Business Standard, Moneycontrol, Financial Express, Lapaas Voice, Yahoo Finance, MSN, Discovery Alert
